title: Improving flood detection with large-scale dashboard camera data
authors: Franchi, M., Garg, N., Ju, W., Pierson, E.

figure.caption: The BayFlood pipeline as stacked map layers: raw dashcam images across New York City are labelled flooded or not flooded by a vision-language model, checked against external flood data (sensors, 311 reports, stormwater maps), and combined into a flood estimate for every Census tract.
figure.credit: Figure 1 from Franchi et al. (2026), Nature Communications, CC BY 4.0.

tldr: Ordinary dashboard-camera photos, read by an off-the-shelf vision-language model and combined with a spatial Bayesian model, can map street flooding across a whole city and reveal flooded neighbourhoods that sensors and resident reports miss.
background: Cities usually learn where streets flood from three sources: fixed flood sensors, resident complaints (such as New York's 311 line) and physics-based stormwater maps. Sensors are too few to cover every street, complaints depend on who chooses to report, and stormwater maps assume rainfall that does not match any real storm. Dashcams on commercial and ride-share cars photograph streets continuously, but training a flood detector normally needs a large labelled dataset, which is hard to build because flooded images are rare.
approach: The authors used about 1.44 million dashcam images supplied by the company Nexar, mainly 926,212 daytime images from New York City during the 29 September 2023 storm, plus three other storm days in New York and the San Francisco Bay Area. Each image was classified without any task-specific training by the open-source vision-language model Cambrian-1-13B, which was asked whether the street showed more than a foot of standing water. One thousand of the classified images were checked by hand, and a spatial Bayesian model then combined the model labels, these human checks and nearby-tract information to estimate the fraction of flooded images in each Census tract. The resulting map was compared with 311 reports, FloodNet sensor locations, stormwater accumulation zones, catch basins and elevation.
findings: Only 0.2% of the New York images were classified as flooded; 65.8% of those were truly flooded, while just 0.6% of images classified as dry actually showed flooding, so a 'flooded' label made flooding about 110 times more likely.
The zero-shot model beat other open-source vision-language models, a fine-tuned ResNet and GPT-4o-mini, and kept strong signal on the other storm days and in San Francisco.

Tracts the method flagged as high risk were 1.9 times likelier to have a FloodNet sensor and 1.3 times likelier to have a 311 flood report, and their minimum elevation was 2.0 times lower, even though the model was not given these data.
About 1.05 million New Yorkers (12% of the city) live in high-risk tracts; 100,150 of them live where none of the existing methods (sensors, 311 or stormwater maps) indicated flood risk.

After accounting for estimated flooding, wealthier tracts and those with more White residents and fewer Hispanic residents were more likely to file 311 reports, and the authors used the maps to suggest 25 new sensor sites to the FloodNet team.
relevance: Urban flash floods, like those in Seoul's low-lying districts during intense monsoon downpours, often hit streets long before any gauge or official report notices them. This study shows that cameras already moving through the city, such as dashcams, CCTV or delivery vehicles, can act as a dense flood-monitoring network without costly labelling, and it reminds us that complaint-based data can under-represent vulnerable neighbourhoods. For students and engineers it is a practical template for combining AI image classification with simple statistics and a small amount of human checking; for city managers it points to fairer ways to choose where sensors and drainage upgrades go.

title: Short-term drought forecasting in Iran using multi-source machine learning: an assessment of autoregressive, teleconnection-driven, and hybrid paradigms
authors: Jian, J., Mahmoudi, P., Jafari, P., Ghaemi, A., Yang, J., Firoozi, F.
journal: Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences

figure.caption: Workflow of the study: monthly rainfall is turned into the SPI drought index, combined with climate-index inputs under three scenarios, and fed to nine machine- and deep-learning models whose 1–3-month forecasts are scored with R², MSE and MAE.
figure.credit: Figure 3 from Jian et al. (2026), Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences, CC BY 4.0.

tldr: For month-ahead drought forecasts in Iran, there is no single best recipe: mixing a station's own drought history with global climate indices works best in dry inland areas, while either source alone wins in certain coastal or local climates.
background: Drought forecasters usually pick one of two kinds of inputs: the recent history of the drought index itself (its 'memory'), or large-scale climate signals such as ENSO or the NAO that steer rainfall from far away. Each approach has worked in local case studies, but nobody had compared them, and their combination, side by side across a large and climatically diverse country. Iran, which ranges from hyper-arid deserts to very wet Caspian coasts, is a natural test bed for that question.
approach: The authors used 30 years (1993–2022) of quality-checked monthly rainfall from 96 synoptic stations and computed the Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI). They built three input scenarios: S1 used 19 global teleconnection indices lagged 1–3 months; S2 used past SPI values with memory lengths of 3, 6, 9 or 12 months; S3 combined the climate indices with 3 or 6 months of SPI history. Nine algorithms, from linear regression and KNN to Random Forest, gradient boosting, XGBoost, Bayesian ridge regression and LSTM, forecast SPI 1, 2 and 3 months ahead and were scored with R², MSE and MAE. They also repeated runs 20 times at two contrasting stations to check how stable each model was.
findings: With climate indices alone (S1), Random Forest was the most reliable model, and in the northwest, Caspian coast and western Zagros it explained up to about half of the SPI variance one month ahead (R² of 0.57 at Anzali), but skill dropped sharply at 2–3 months.
With drought history alone (S2), longer memory helped: feeding 12 months of past SPI gave the best results, and LSTM was the top model in this setting.
The hybrid setting (S3) won across much of the arid and semi-arid central plateau; at Isfahan it reached R² = 0.65 with MSE = 0.36, beating both single-source options.

Some places preferred a single source: climate indices worked best at Chabahar (R² = 0.49) and Anzali, while drought history alone was best at Ahvaz (R² = 0.55), and each station's winning setup rarely changed at longer lead times.
Across 20 repeated runs, Random Forest gave the most consistent scores, while LSTM and the polynomial SVM varied more from run to run.
relevance: Drought early warning is only useful if forecasts are trustworthy where people actually live and farm, and this study shows that the best forecasting setup can change from one region to the next. Korea faces a similar mix of influences, with monsoon rainfall, typhoons and dry springs shaped by both local persistence and large-scale signals like ENSO, so a 'one model for the whole country' approach may leave some basins poorly served. A practical lesson for students and water managers is to test several input designs and keep a simple, stable model such as Random Forest as a strong baseline before turning to more complex deep learning.

title: How well do hydrological models simulate streamflow extremes and drought-to-flood transitions?
authors: Muñoz-Castro, E., Anderson, B. J., Astagneau, P. C., Swain, D. L., Mendoza, P. A., Brunner, M. I.

figure.caption: Detected droughts (red shading), floods (blue) and the time between them: a rapid drought-to-flood transition in the Biobío River, Chile (a), and a seasonal one in the Dischma River, Switzerland (b).
figure.credit: Figure 3 from Muñoz-Castro et al. (2026), Hydrology and Earth System Sciences, CC BY 4.0.

tldr: A model with a high KGE can still miss floods and drought-to-flood switches — extremes need to be checked on their own.
background: A drought that suddenly flips into a flood can do more damage than either extreme alone: dry soils, low reservoirs and drought-mode operations leave little room to respond. Hydrological models are the main tool for studying such transitions, but they are usually calibrated and judged with aggregate scores such as the Kling–Gupta efficiency (KGE), which say little about how well individual extreme events are reproduced.
approach: The authors calibrated four conceptual rainfall–runoff models (GR4J, GR5J, GR6J and TUW) in 63 catchments in Chile and Switzerland, trying several calibration set-ups: KGE variants, streamflow transformations and component weights. Droughts and floods were picked out with thresholds, a transition was defined as a drought followed by a flood within a set window (rapid: under 14 days; seasonal: under 90 days), and detection skill was scored with the Critical Success Index (CSI). ANOVA and correlation analysis then separated the effects of model structure, calibration choices and catchment attributes.
findings: A high KGE does not guarantee good event detection: median CSI was around 0.5 for droughts but only about 0.2–0.3 for floods and for transitions.
Droughts are captured better than floods, rapid (under 14-day) transitions are the hardest, and skill depends mainly on getting the timing right.
Model structure matters most, followed by the streamflow transformation used in calibration; the KGE formulation and weights matter less.
Skill is lowest in semi-arid, high-mountain and flashy catchments, pointing to weak representation of soil-moisture and near-surface processes.
relevance: Flood warnings, drought plans and climate-impact studies all lean on hydrological models, so a model that looks good on average but misses the extremes can give false confidence exactly when it matters. In Korea, dry springs that switch into heavy monsoon floods are a familiar pattern, and this kind of transition is where the paper finds models weakest. For anyone building or using such models — students, researchers or water managers — the lesson is simple: check the extremes and the switches between them directly, not just the overall score.
